title: Supporting Learning During Educational Adaptation: Supervisor Autonomy Support, Basic Psychological Need Satisfaction, and Academic Achievement in International Graduate Students
abstract: International graduate students must learn while adapting to an unfamiliar academic and cultural environment, yet the instructional conditions that sustain that learning remain poorly specified. Grounded in self-determination theory (SDT) and in research on the non-intellective correlates of academic performance, this study examined whether supervisor autonomy support—an aspect of teacher cognition and instructional decision-making—is associated with academic achievement through the satisfaction of basic psychological needs, which SDT treats as the proximal motivational condition for self-regulated learning. Because self-regulated learning and metacognition were not measured, this study tests the motivational preconditions of cognition rather than cognitive processes themselves. A cross-sectional online survey was completed by 95 international graduate students enrolled in Chinese universities, who responded to the Supervisor Autonomy Support Scale, the Basic Psychological Needs Scale, and the Graduate Student Academic Achievement Scale. After demographic controls, supervisor autonomy support positively predicted need satisfaction (B = 0.232, β = 0.421, p = 0.001) and academic achievement (B = 0.474, β = 0.541, p < 0.001) and need satisfaction positively predicted academic achievement (B = 0.373, β = 0.234, p < 0.01). Structural equation modelling with 5000 bootstrap resamples indicated that need satisfaction carried part of this association (indirect effect = 0.112, bias-corrected 95% CI [0.045, 0.207]; direct effect = 0.572, 95% CI [0.438, 0.706]); the mediation is therefore partial, and the width of the indirect-effect interval indicates that its magnitude is estimated imprecisely. Given the cross-sectional, single-source design and the self-reported nature of academic achievement, these findings are interpreted as associations consistent with the hypothesised mediation rather than as evidence of an established causal mechanism. Autonomy-supportive supervision is therefore a low-cost, trainable route for establishing the cognitive-motivational conditions that support learning during educational adaptation, with implications for the assessment and design of graduate supervision.
